system.summary: Each number 1-682 is the position of a character in 13 printed lines of Dumas's 1775 preface to Vattel, Le Droit des gens; every occurrence of a letter is an alternative number for it.

diacritics.note: Accents ignored in use; apostrophes, hyphens, commas, full stops, & and the reference mark are counted as characters and used.

prior_solution.where: The key and system: Dumas's letter of 30 April 1776 (Franklin Papers 22:403-412) and S. Tomokiyo, Cryptiana, 'Dumas' Cipher - Benjamin Franklin's Favorite Cipher' (2008-09), who re-established Dumas's own key text of 1776 from the Committee's enciphering table. Decoded passages in print: Franklin Papers 22, Sparks 9, Force 5th ser. 2, Wharton 2-4. Contemporary decipherments interlined on most pages (unpublished for the passages the editions leave out).

conditions.human_role: Andrew Beling directed the research and set the contribution scope; the work was done with AI agents.
tools: Python transcription-reconciliation, decoding and test scripts (scripts/, key/, tests/)
image crops of the NARA Catalog images

solution.what: Fetched PCC item 93 vol. 1 (503 images) and the M332 roll 2 Dumas file (211 images) from the NARA Catalog at a person's pace; item 93 vols. 2-4 screened on contact sheets only.
Found the key system in Dumas's 30 April 1776 letter (line totals, counting rule) and Tomokiyo's transcription of the 13 key lines on Cryptiana.
Built the 682-position key from the 1830 reprint of the preface adjusted to Dumas's line totals and Tomokiyo's wording; froze it (sha256 36276e0a...).

Test 1: key built from the 1778 glosses on M332 images 9, 10, 13 predicted the glosses on image 20: 106 of 108 (200 shuffled keys: mean 7.9%, max 14.8%). Test 2 (plan written first): the printed-text key against the glosses on item 93 image 173: 129 of 134 (129 of 130 sure glosses); 200 shuffled keys mean 7.1%, max 14.9%.
Every cipher run transcribed twice by independent passes (forward and backward), about 6,900 number places; about 95% agreed before image checks; the rest settled on crops.
Decoded and read all 21 items; emendations marked; print checked passage by passage in the Franklin Papers (partly), Sparks 9 and Wharton 2-3.

A second AI agent of ours rebuilt the key from Cryptiana (one difference in 682, position 515, a typing slip on the page), transcribed four passages on its own with the same numbers and readings, and redid the print check in Wharton 2-4, Sparks 9 and Force. Corrections applied: 1776 despatch D images 52-53 are in Force; 641 is the V. of 'Madam V. Loder'; 2 Aug 1777 L12 is 14, not 12; wording of May 1779 and 20 Sept 1779.

Statistical validation (docs/_validate.py): 4129 tokens, 678 types, fr-1750-nospace order 4: reading -2.008 per letter; random keys -5.269 (z 39.7); key annealed onto shuffled ciphertext best -3.454 (mean -3.482, z 85.9); annealer on the real text -3.528. Verdict: pass.

validation.notes: claimed per-occurrence score -2.008; polyphony 0.0; 1 unread tokens left out; annealer on the real text from random keys reached -3.528

outcome.method_basis: Key text and system from Dumas's 1776 letter and Tomokiyo's transcription, tested against the contemporary glosses; every cipher run in the Dumas letters of PCC item 93 vol. 1 and M332 roll 2 transcribed twice and decoded.

credits.note: Andrew Beling, with AI agents: inventory of every cipher passage in the Dumas letters of PCC item 93 vol. 1 and M332 roll 2, double transcriptions, the test of the printed key against the contemporary glosses, and the text of the passages the editions leave out. Reading with a known key, not a break.

The Committee's decipherer or decipherers, who wrote letters over the numbers on most pages (faint pencil in 1776, ink later). Hand not identified; the letter forms are compatible with James Lovell's, which is not an identification. Their glosses were used to test the key and to settle doubtful numbers.

Member of the Committee of Secret Correspondence to which the 1776 despatches were addressed; Dumas set out the key and the counting rule for it in his letter of 30 April 1776; Franklin used the cipher himself (to Dumas, 16 Aug 1781).

Satoshi Tomokiyo, Cryptiana, 'Dumas' Cipher - Benjamin Franklin's Favorite Cipher' (2008-09): re-established Dumas's own 13-line key text of 1776 from the Committee's enciphering table, the line totals and the homophonic system. Our key agrees with his page in 681 of 682 positions (515, a typing slip on the page).

Papers of Benjamin Franklin vol. 22: the 30 April and 14 May 1776 letters with the cipher passages decoded in brackets, from the interlined decoding. Two readings corrected here: "France" for "fiance" (571 = r, glossed r); "Les alliés" for "Des alliés" (70 = l by the key; the contemporary gloss looks like d, so the slip was the decipherer's and the editors followed it).
Diplomatic Correspondence of the American Revolution vol. 9: translations including the decoded content of the printed letters; leaves out the passages listed in NOTES.
American Archives, 5th ser., vol. 2, cols. 99-103: despatch D of Sept-Oct 1776 with the numbers, an interlined decipherment and a translation (images 52-53, "le ministre même", "Madam V. Loder").
Revolutionary Diplomatic Correspondence vols. 2-4: translations of the printed letters, the cipher content included where Sparks had it; lists the omitted letters of 1777.

texts.summary: Dumas reports opening himself to a French minister at The Hague, the request for French mediation or a Bourbon alliance, and the minister's fear that reconciled colonies would turn on their helpers. Printed decoded in the Franklin Papers 22:403-412.
